channel.title: Ahmed Mostafa: Notes on product thinking
channel.description: Short, practical notes on product work in regulated and enterprise contexts, by Ahmed Mostafa.

item.title: Your backlog is a contract, not a to-do list
item.description: In a regulated product, every user story is an agreement between compliance, engineering, and the business. Treating the backlog that way is what actually cuts rework.

item.title: Turning a sprawling API into a five-step wizard
item.description: A real client PRD, reverse-engineered. How I turned a large, prerequisite-heavy Meta API surface into a flow a non-technical founder could finish without a manual.

item.title: What an engineering background changes, and what it doesn't
item.description: Not the cliches. The specific, concrete ways an Electronics and Communications Engineering background changes how I pressure-test feasibility and talk to engineering teams.

item.title: The stakeholder map nobody draws
item.description: In a regulated fintech product, legal, compliance, delivery, and ops all have to say yes before a feature ships. Here's the map I actually use, and why silence isn't a signature.

item.title: Your pricing dashboard is a trust problem, not a data problem
item.description: Pricing and operational dashboards fail for a different reason than most PMs think. It's rarely the data. It's who's allowed to disagree with what the dashboard says.

item.title: The best scope cuts happen in discovery, not sprint three
item.description: Discovery sessions are where scope gaps are cheapest to find. Most teams find them in sprint three instead, after they've already been built around.

item.title: A curriculum is a product roadmap wearing a different outfit
item.description: Designing a coding and robotics curriculum for K-12 students taught me more about roadmapping under real constraints than most software projects have.

item.title: I learned product-market fit before I had the words for it
item.description: Years before I could define product-market fit, I was doing a version of it: matching training programs to what students actually needed, not what looked good in a brochure.
